title: Chimichurri
subtitle: Argentine herb sauce for grilled meat
excerpt: A bright, punchy sauce of parsley, garlic, oil and vinegar that is the essential companion to Argentine grilled meat. It takes 10 minutes to make and no cooking at all. Make it a few hours ahead so the flavours have time to develop.
sourceNotes: Chimichurri is the defining condiment of Argentine and Uruguayan cooking, served alongside asado (grilled meat). The origin of the name is disputed; some link it to Basque immigrants, others to British settlers. Whatever its etymology, the sauce has been central to River Plate cooking for well over a century.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to 2 days ahead and refrigerate in a jar. The flavour deepens with time. Bring to room temperature before serving.

content.text: This makes enough chimichurri for 8 and takes about 10 minutes. There is no cooking involved. The sauce is simply a matter of chopping the herbs finely, mixing everything together and leaving it to sit for a while. The longer it rests, the more the garlic and chilli mellow into the oil.

Chop the herbs by hand rather than blending them. A blender makes a smooth paste rather than a rustic herb sauce, and the texture is part of what makes chimichurri what it is. Flat-leaf parsley is non-negotiable; curly parsley has a different, more bitter flavour. The coriander is optional and not traditional in Argentina, but adds a fresh note that many people like. Taste before serving and adjust the vinegar and chilli to your preference.

items.prepNote: or use a light olive oil

content.text: Finely chop a large bunch of flat-leaf parsley (leaves and tender stalks). You want about 30g of chopped parsley in total.
Combine the parsley, coriander (if using), minced garlic, 2 tbsp red wine vinegar, 1 tsp dried oregano and 1 tsp chilli flakes in a bowl.
Pour over the oil and lime juice (or the additional 2 tbsp red wine vinegar). Stir well and season with salt.
Taste and adjust: more vinegar for sharpness, more chilli for heat, more salt if it tastes flat. Leave to rest for at least 30 minutes before serving so the garlic softens in the acid.
Serve at room temperature alongside grilled steak, chicken or vegetables. Stir again just before serving as the oil will have separated.

attrs.cause: Fresh garlic is very pungent before it has had time to mellow in the acid
attrs.fix: Let the sauce rest for at least 1 hour, or ideally overnight in the fridge. The acidity of the vinegar softens raw garlic significantly.
Add more red wine vinegar a teaspoon at a time, tasting after each addition. A pinch more salt and a squeeze of lime will also brighten the flavour.

attrs.symptom: Herbs have turned dark and muddy
attrs.cause: The acid in the vinegar has begun to break down the chlorophyll in the herbs over time
attrs.fix: Make chimichurri within 2 days of using. Store it in the fridge but bring to room temperature before serving. After 2 days the flavour remains good but the colour dulls.

content.text: In Argentina, chimichurri sits on the table at every asado alongside the meat. It is a condiment rather than a marinade, although some people use it as both. Each family has its own version: some make it wetter, some drier, some add more chilli, some none at all. The only rule that holds everywhere is that the herbs must be fresh and the parsley must be flat-leaf.
